title: Forces & free-body diagrams
description: Start with a sketch, name the forces, and make the system easier to reason about.
sourceFiles: CRAMMED demonstration notes — not course material

sections.title: A force is more than a number
sections.body: A force is a vector: it has both magnitude and direction. Its SI unit is the newton (N). When several forces act on a body, their vector sum is the resultant force.

sections.title: Resolve before you add
sections.body: Resolving a force means replacing it with perpendicular components whose vector sum is the original force.

sections.title: Components at an angle
sections.body:
For a force F at angle θ above the horizontal:
Fₓ = F cos θ
Fᵧ = F sin θ

sections.title: Pulling a loaded cart
sections.body: Pull with 10 N at 30° above horizontal. The forward component is 10 cos 30° ≈ 8.7 N; the upward component is 10 sin 30° = 5 N. Resolve first so each direction can be analysed separately.

sections.title: Angle check
sections.body: These component formulas assume θ is measured from the horizontal. If the angle is measured from the vertical, the sine and cosine roles swap.

sections.title: 30-second recap
sections.body: Forces are vectors. Choose axes, resolve each force into components, then add components along each axis.

sections.title: Isolate the object
items: Choose the body you are analysing.
Represent it simply and show only forces acting on that body.
Label each force with its direction and a clear name.
Choose useful coordinate axes before resolving angled forces.

sections.title: A useful boundary
sections.body: A free-body diagram shows the external forces acting on one selected body, not the forces that body exerts on everything else.

sections.title: On a level table
sections.body: For a stationary block on a level table, show its weight downward and the table's normal contact force upward. Add other forces only if they act on the block.

sections.title: Common omission
sections.body: Do not draw a force just because it appears in the story. Check whether it acts on the selected object.

sections.title: 30-second recap
sections.body: One body, external forces only, directions labelled. A clean diagram is a map for the equations that follow.

sections.title: No change in motion
sections.body: For a body in static equilibrium, the resultant force is zero and the resultant moment about any point is zero.

sections.title: A balanced beam
sections.body: A light 2 m beam is supported at its centre, with a 10 N weight 1 m to each side. The moments are equal and opposite (10 N·m each), and the support supplies 20 N upward to balance the two weights.

sections.title: Keep the conditions together
sections.body: Force balance alone does not guarantee rotational equilibrium. Include a moment balance when the body can rotate.

sections.title: 30-second recap
sections.body: Static equilibrium needs both translational and rotational balance: zero resultant force and zero resultant moment.

questions.prompt: A 10 N force acts at 30° above the horizontal. Which expression gives its horizontal component?
questions.explanation: When the angle is measured from the horizontal, the horizontal component is adjacent to the angle: F cos θ.

questions.prompt: What belongs on a free-body diagram of a block on a table?
options: Forces the block exerts on the table
Only external forces acting on the block
Every force mentioned in the problem
questions.explanation: A free-body diagram isolates one body and shows the external forces acting on that body.

questions.prompt: A body is in static equilibrium in a plane. Which set of conditions is appropriate?
questions.explanation: Planar static equilibrium requires balance in both translation directions and rotation.

questions.prompt: An angle is given from the vertical instead of the horizontal. What should you do before resolving a force?
options: Check which component is adjacent to the stated angle
questions.explanation: Sine and cosine depend on the reference angle; identify the adjacent and opposite components first.
